meta.split: 5 planted deficits over 32 novice cases (16 novices vs 8 experts); cluster bootstrap by person, B = 2000
meta.note: Which deficit was injected, and what it costs. Detected = the alignment attributes at least X seconds to the right cog family, X = max(1 s, 95th percentile of what the same procedure attributes when two experts are compared). In this data the placebo attributes at most 0.0 s to any family, so X is the 1 s floor for every deficit. Synthetic apprentices with a known price per trace; this shows the method recovers what we planted.

rows.label: Reads the result again and again

deficit_recovery.detection_rule: detected when recovered seconds >= X; X = max(1 s, 95th percentile of the placebo attribution to that cog family); precision and recall are pooled over every (case, deficit) pair
deficit_recovery.price_definition: seconds the deficit added minus seconds it removed, against the same case without it (exact by construction)
deficit_recovery.reference: nearest expert by alignment cost, never the same person

meta.split: cluster bootstrap by person, B = 2000; null = 1000 permutations of the expert/novice label across people
meta.note: Real gap = novice minus nearest-expert seconds per case, mean over people. Placebo = each expert against the nearest other expert. Null = labels shuffled across people, whole procedure repeated (interval = 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the permutation distribution). Both controls should include zero; the real gap should not.

null_placebo.unit: seconds per case, novice minus reference

meta.note: 7376 scored 30-second bins from 2676 episodes; label = no progress in the next 60 s.

hazard.interval_note: Intervals resample episodes (clusters) within the pooled held-out predictions; they do not capture person-to-person variation (see per_person).
caveats: Labels and events are defined from `progress` events in the data; the model predicts 'no progress in the next 60 s', not 'the person is confused'.
Intervals resample episodes, not people; with few people the person-level spread (per_person) is the honest uncertainty.

Alarm threshold is chosen on training people only under the false-alarm budget; it can overshoot on the held-out person (see false_alarms_within_budget). The budget is a design choice, not a measured tolerance of real workers.
Synthetic origin: results show the pipeline recovers planted structure, not that real people behave this way.

limitations.text: Hazard, skills, policy, routing and agent-claim results come from synthetic personas, scripted apprentices or simulators we wrote. They show that the methods recover structure we planted, not that real workers behave this way.
The stuck hazard is evaluated on four synthetic personas, so 'held-out person' means one of four. Intervals resample episodes, not people; the per-person spread is the honest uncertainty.

Probabilities are better than the baselines and calibrated, but alert quality is modest: about a third of stuck events are flagged, and on held-out people the false-alarm rate (about 1.2 per hour) overshoots the 1 per hour budget chosen on training people.
'Stuck' means no progress event in the next 60 seconds, which is not the same as confusion. Fast thinking and slow typing both look stuck to this label.
The apprentice traces follow a fixed task script, so part of the hazard model's large gain on them is learning the script, not predicting stuck. The four-persona result is the headline.

meta.note: Value of the rule-baseline policy estimated from logs of a different policy. The true value is known because the simulator is ours.

caveats: Synthetic simulator: the reward structure is invented by us. It shows the estimators recover a known truth, not that the real reward looks like this.
Implicit labels (followed, dismissed, repeated, undone) are noisy proxies for 'did it help'; the reward model weights them by assumption.
Intervals hold the cross-fitted reward model fixed and resample decisions; they do not include the variance of re-fitting it.
Doubly robust needs correct logged propensities. The simulator logs them exactly; in a live system a logging bug would break every estimate here.
Weights reach 20 (propensity floor 0.05); effective sample size is reported with each target.

meta.note: Auto-approve the safest households, send the rest to an expert. Cases are synthetic sandbox households scored by the three sandbox calculators' own rules; the reference is a simplified internal rule set, not law.

routing.bound_held_definition: the held-out data does not contradict 'true error rate of the auto-approved set <= alpha': the lower end of its Clopper-Pearson interval is not above alpha
caveats: CIRCULARITY: the calculators' quirks (site b ignores capital tariff income; site c applies a two-child limit and treats exactly 16,000 as over the limit) and the household archetypes that trigger them were planted by us. The router can only show it found our planted structure; it does not show that real calculators or real agents fail this way.

The reference answer is the sandbox oracle, a simplified internal rule set loosely shaped like a Universal Credit award. It is not law and not PolicyEngine; 'error' means 'differs from that oracle by more than one pound'.

The stand-in agent is a rule over the three calculator answers (the one at least two agree on, else the mean); no model was run. With the median of three the agent is never wrong on these households (nothing to route), and with the plain mean the label is 'any calculator disagrees', which the spread feature predicts directly (see stand_ins).
Stated confidence is a function of calculator disagreement only, so it carries no information the spread does not.

The label is almost a deterministic function of the features (a three-way calculator disagreement), so a log loss and ECE near zero reflect separability, not skilful calibration. Compare coverage with the spread-only baseline: the router adds little over it here.
Errors are concentrated in one archetype (see case_set.errors_by_archetype), so the effective number of independent error patterns is small.
Expert review time per case is an assumption, not a measurement.
The guarantee covers exchangeable households like these; a new rule or calculator breaks it silently.

limitations.text: Hazard, skills, policy, routing and agent-claim results come from synthetic personas, scripted apprentices or simulators we wrote. They show that the methods recover structure we planted, not that real workers behave this way.

The router finding those quirks shows it recovers our planted structure, not that real calculators or real agents fail this way; the task is nearly deterministic, and the plain spread of calculator answers does almost as well.

The routing error bound holds for cases like the ones used to calibrate it. A new benefit rule, calculator site or household type breaks that assumption silently. Review time per case is an assumption.

meta.split: simulated workdays; buy cost b = 16 manual runs; forecast sees 10 workdays, cost over the next 50
meta.note: Regret = cost divided by the hindsight-best cost (1.0 is perfect). Simulated mechanism; not real build decisions.

limitations.text: Ski-rental regret is measured on simulated routines (lognormal run rates, 45% retiring after an exponential life, the forecast sees 10 workdays), not on real build decisions. It shows the rule's behaviour against break-even under a stated mechanism.

The rule is not the best everywhere. Lowest regret by build cost: b=4: Build now (1.07); b=8: Build now (1.15); b=16: Build now (1.27); b=32: Ski rental with predictions (lambda 0.2) (1.33). When building is cheap (b = 4 manual runs) building at once (1.07) is level with the rule (1.07) and both are ahead of break-even (1.70); the prediction earns its keep when building costs more. The pack's own build costs are 4 to 9 runs.
The trust parameter lambda is fixed by us (or set from past forecast error by a heuristic that is not in the paper). It was not tuned on this simulation.

meta.split: forward held-out days within each persona
meta.note: Synthetic personas, 21 days each. Pooled means of per-persona results; per-persona detail and intervals in the full dict.

limitations.text: Presence results come from 4 synthetic personas of 21 days each, not from real people. The schedule change on day 15 is planted; the real change in a person's week will not look like it.

The weekly map predicts held-out days worse than a simple baseline for shift-worker (map Brier 0.214 against prior 0.194 and one global rate 0.175). A weekly template does not suit rotating shifts or no routine.
The window forecast is only roughly calibrated: expected calibration error 0.07 to 0.13 across personas on held-out days, and it beats pooled survival (no time of week) on 2 of 4 personas.
The 95% intervals on the presence map contain the planted active probability in only 55% to 91% of bins. Smoothing across neighbouring bins trades bias for variance, so the intervals are too narrow.

Idle capacity per week is over-estimated: nine-to-five 12 h against a planted 10 h; irregular 10 h against a planted 6 h. With no sleep event the machine is assumed to stay on for 60 minutes after the last event, and a locked screen still counts as idle although a desktop run cannot start on it.

The start-or-wait rule is conservative: it collided with the worker's return in 2.1% of started runs against an allowed 10%, and used 74% of idle time against 90% for running whenever idle five minutes. Runs are replayed one per decision point on held-out spells; interruption and idle-use intervals count spells as independent.

meta.split: planted routines per persona, found by the routine finder
meta.note: Precision is over proposals (after the value gate); recall over planted routines with at least 3 runs.

limitations.text: Routine precision and recall are scored on 4 synthetic personas whose routines were planted by a generator that varies steps and timing but not the way real people drift. They show the method recovers planted structure, not that real routines look like this.

The finder alone (minimum support 3) returns many small clusters of one-off work: precision 22% over 55 clusters. The value gate removes them: precision 100% over 6 proposals. Short routines of three or four steps are the hardest to tell from chance.
Planted routines that ran fewer than 3 times cannot be found by design and are excluded from recall: nine-to-five/weekly-report.

meta.note: How well a claimed success that code has not yet checked can be trusted. Synthetic runs.

caveats: Synthetic runs generated from a known mechanism; real agent traces will differ and this has not been validated on them.
Features are trace summaries, not content; claims about page text cannot be assessed here.
Code still decides success. A low predicted risk never replaces the completion check.

pooling.note: Cold-start error is predictive log loss (nats per trial, lower is better) on the person's later episodes, leave one person out. Partial pooling shrinks a new person toward the role's rate and trusts their own data more as it accumulates. `ci` is the interval for the partial-pooling value; `*_minus_partial` shows how much worse each alternative is, with its own interval.
pooling.split: leave-one-person-out; scored on episodes after the first max(k)

meta.note: Cold start for a new worker: error after 0, 1, 3 and 10 of their own episodes. Four synthetic personas.

headline.quantity: stuck base rate (share of 30 s bins with no progress in the next 60 s)

limitations.text: Hazard, skills, policy, routing and agent-claim results come from synthetic personas, scripted apprentices or simulators we wrote. They show that the methods recover structure we planted, not that real workers behave this way.

Cold-start priors are built from four synthetic personas (or 24 scripted apprentices with two cases each); with so few and such alike people, partial pooling is hard to tell from complete pooling, and learning-curve drift is not modelled.

caveats: The primary result has four personas, so 'the role' is three other people; between-persona spread is small, which pushes partial pooling toward complete pooling. The apprentice rows have 24 people but only two episodes each.
Deficit rows read the planted deficits from truth.json, as if the genome module had detected them perfectly.
Learners' true deficit rates fall with practice, so every static estimate, pooled or not, is biased for later cases; pooling does not fix drift.
Intervals resample scored episodes with each person's estimate held fixed; they do not capture person-to-person variation beyond what those episodes show.

Bins within an episode are correlated, so bin-level counts overstate the information in a person's data; the empirical-Bayes prior fitted on them is therefore a little too tight about each person's own rate.

meta.note: Scripted vulnerable planner and mock reader: measures the layers, not a real model. 42 attacks, 31 clean pages (10 hard negatives); each case runs once per configuration. Includes 5 supplemental built-in attacks (settings tampering, raw actions) that the committed catalog does not contain; `committed_only` reports the committed catalog alone.

limitations.text: The planner is a script that follows any instruction it can see. These numbers measure what the layers stop, not how a real model behaves under attack.
Attacks are synthetic and were written by the same team that wrote the defences. A new attack style can get through.
Layer 1 (sanitising) is modelled as defeating only markup-based attacks (fake system tags, tool-call syntax); a scripted planner that follows plain text shows no change when it is off.
Layers overlap, so leaving one out often changes nothing. The 'only_<layer>' rows show each layer's standalone strength.
A detector hit pauses the run for a human, so task success under attack is lower than on clean pages by design.

Removing the injection detector did not let any attack through in this test, but it lets far more tasks finish (the reader alone keeps the planner clean). The detector's job is to catch an attack early, and its price is pauses.

Data-flow rules and the goal check cannot tell an exfiltration request to an endpoint on a site the routine already uses from normal browsing there. Only the detector and the reader stop that kind of attack.

Real data is thin: the only real signal is the team's own machine timestamps (times only, collected with consent). There are no real benefits-processor traces, so nothing here has been validated on real casework.

The entitlement figures the agent is scored against come from a simplified internal rule set, not the law. It agrees with PolicyEngine UK within 1 pound on only 8 of 20 generated households, so passing our oracle is not the same as getting the entitlement right.

Section 'study' has no numbers: the live study has not been run: no data in evals/study/results/.

The three calculators are sandbox sites we built, each with planted quirks, and each computes one Universal-Credit-shaped entitlement. They say nothing about how real calculators behave or what their terms and bot protection allow.
Agent-claim calibration uses simulated runs until real agent runs exist. A low predicted risk of a false claim never replaces the code check, which decides success.

The off-hours live run depends on the conditions spike S2 passed under: macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording granted, an unlocked screen, a harmless app, the owner present. The apprentice traces follow a fixed task script, so part of the hazard model's large gain on them is learning the script, not predicting stuck. The four-persona result is the headline.

Skill tracing saturates on synthetic personas (about 35 tasks a day): mastery reaches its ceiling on day one and cannot follow the planted learning curve. Decay with absence is shown in unit tests only.

On the learner trajectories (three learners, thirty cases each, one with a three-day absence) the help level does lighten as deficits fade, but a clock alone ranks the true curve as well as mastery does, the ranking of which deficits fade fastest is near chance, and the short absence did not move the level. Three learners make every interval wide.

The 95% forecast interval covered what happened in 8 of 11 planted routines (73%), which is below nominal and rests on one held-out week; the schedule change on day 15 falls inside it, and the model has no way to know about it.

The recovered price differs from the planted price, with an interval that excludes zero, for: repeated_read_result (+13.5 s, interval 5.1 to 23.3). The alignment names a block of extra steps by its content, so a deficit that shares steps with another is mis-priced.
